# Review: 2028 Volvo’s XC60/90 PHEVs get 80 miles of EV range, changing the game
Volvo flew us out to Copenhagen to drive across the bridge to Sweden to check out the upcoming 2028 XC60 and XC90 plug-in hybrids. The new vehicles promise to double the EV-only range to 73-78 miles, making them a new breed of hybrid rarely seen outside China. But what can you do with so much EV-only range?

Volvo’s upcoming 2028 XC60 T8 and XC90 T8 “Long-Range” PHEVs are the rare exception that actually force us to pay attention. By stuffing a **41.2 kWh floor-mounted battery** (37.9 kWh usable) into its solid but aging SPA1 platform, Volvo has more than doubled the electric range of its two bestselling SUVs. Both now have more battery capacity and range than the original all-electric Nissan Leaf, Hyundai Ioniq, and many of the compliance EVs that followed. Volvo also doubled the charging speed from 3.6kW to a more reasonable 7.2 kW, meaning charge times are roughly unchanged.

The real headline, though, is the electric range:
- **2028 XC60 T8:** Up to **78 miles** of preliminary EPA-estimated EV range (590 miles combined) and **67 MPGe**.
- **2028 XC90 T8:** Up to **73 miles** of preliminary EPA-estimated EV range and **61 MPGe**.

# 2028 Volvo XC90 Long-Range PHEV First Drive: Teaching An Old Hybrid New Long-Range Tricks
Roger Biermann is an automotive journalist of 13 years and has been the Managing Editor at CarBuzz since 2021. With no formal post-high school education, Roger launched his career as an automotive journalist by test driving cars at dealerships and putting his thoughts online before launching his own website in 2012 and running Torquing Cars until he made the move to CarBuzz full-time in 2019.

So the question I sought to answer when I flew to Copenhagen, Denmark last week was whether Volvo could innovate enough to keep the aging [XC90](https://carbuzz.com/cars/volvo/xc90/2027/) SUV — now more than a decade into its second generation — fresh and relevant in the face of [new generations of the Audi Q7](https://carbuzz.com/2027-audi-q7-first-drive-review/) and BMW X5, and a [refreshed Mercedes-Benz GLE](https://carbuzz.com/2027-mercedes-benz-gle-gls-first-drive-review/).

As for how it drives, it drives exactly like the old one did, which is to say there's an abundance of power — more than most families will ever need — with the engine kicking in at full throttle to deploy all 455 horsepower and 560 lb-ft. Without it, the rear e-motor alone delivers 174 hp, with the 2.0-liter turbo four-cylinder (the twincharged version is now exclusive to the B6) contributing 247 hp to the total output. Just like before, you can still drive it in one-pedal mode (B drive mode, creep off), which is a novelty for a PHEV and one that bridges the gap between hybrid and electric brilliantly.
